screens.title: ROS Services with Turtlesim
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore ROS services using the simple turtlesim simulator so you can practice real service patterns before moving to physical robots. You will learn which turtlesim services are available, how to call them from the command line, and how to write a client that uses a service to change robot state. We will also examine service design best practices: keeping calls fast, making them idempotent, and providing clear success or error responses. Along the way you'll see a practical example pattern: a battery monitor subscribes to a topic and calls an LED service when the battery is low. That pattern — topic for continuous state, service for discrete commands — is central to many robot systems like gripper control, mode switching, and calibration routines. By the end of this chapter you should be able to call turtlesim services, write simple service clients and servers, and decide when a state-changing operation belongs in a service rather than a topic or an action.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide practice and assessment. First, you will use turtlesim services to teleport, reset, and spawn turtles. Practicing those commands gives you concrete control over simulator state and prepares you to write service clients. Second, you will implement a service-based control system for a simple simulated robot such as a BB-8 or TurtleBot. That means wiring a server to change state and a client or monitor to call those services when needed. Both of these objectives emphasize practical scripting and debugging skills. Third, you will contrast stateless and stateful services so you can choose the right abstraction in your designs. Stateless calls perform an action without depending on current state; stateful calls modify and depend on the simulator or robot state. Finally, you will apply services to real robot scenarios such as LED control, grippers, and mode switching, understanding why services are preferred for discrete, synchronous commands. Each objective maps to hands-on practice: command line calls, Python client code, and a service server skeleton to test.

screens.title: What are ROS services?
screens.narratorSegment: A ROS service is a synchronous, request-response communication primitive for discrete operations. Unlike topics, which stream data continuously, a service call is a single request that expects a specific reply. This makes services ideal for actions like resetting a simulator, spawning a new entity, or switching a robot's operating mode where the caller needs immediate confirmation. For example, in turtlesim the /reset service uses the std_srvs/Empty type and performs a clear reset with no payload. Another example is /spawn: the client sends x, y, theta, and name in the request and receives the created turtle's name in the response. A common misconception is to use services for frequent, high-rate updates; services are not suited for streaming telemetry. If you need continuous feedback, topics or actions are a better fit. Remember that services should be designed to execute quickly — if the task is long-running with feedback, prefer an action. To solidify this concept, try calling /clear and /reset in turtlesim and observe the immediate, synchronous change. What are ROS services? means services are request-response calls for discrete, synchronous commands; use them when the client needs to know the result immediately.. In practical terms, a definition, behavior, and simple examples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What are ROS services?
Formal definition

A service is a synchronous RPC-style primitive in ROS: client sends a typed request and waits for a typed response.

Examples
  • /reset — std_srvs/Empty, resets the simulator.
  • /spawn — turtlesim/Spawn, request includes x, y, theta, name.
  • /set_led — example service for controlling an LED on a robot; expects LED id and on/off.
Key Takeaway

Use services when you need a discrete command and immediate confirmation; do not use them for streaming data.

CLI examples
# Reset the simulation
rosservice call /reset

# Clear the screen
rosservice call /clear

# Spawn a new turtle at (5,5)
rosservice call /spawn "x: 5.0
y: 5.0
theta: 0.0
name: 'turtle2'"
Misconception check: calling a service does not stream updates. If you need continuous feedback, use a topic or an action with feedback.

screens.title: Discovering and calling turtlesim services
screens.narratorSegment: Before you call a service, discover it and inspect its type. Start with rosservice list to see available services and then rosservice type or rosservice info to view the request and response fields. For example, run rosservice list and filter with grep turtlesim to see services like /reset, /spawn, /kill, and /turtle1/teleport_absolute. Once you know the type, craft the right YAML-formatted request and use rosservice call. Practically, spawning a turtle requires sending x, y, theta and name. Teleporting may require floats for x, y, theta depending on the Teleport service definition. A common pitfall is misformatting the YAML payload; watch indentation and quoting for strings. Another pitfall is calling a service before its server is available; use rosservice call only after a node has advertised the service or use rosservice wait. These discovery steps are small but crucial for reliable testing and scripting. Discovering and calling turtlesim services means always inspect available services and their types before calling them; format your request correctly and ensure the server is available.. In practical terms, from rosservice list to rosservice call. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Stateless vs Stateful services
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding whether a service is stateless or stateful helps you reason about consistency and retries. Stateless services perform an action that does not depend on existing internal state. Examples in turtlesim include /reset and /clear: calling them produces the same effect regardless of prior simulator state. These services are easy to reason about and are good candidates for idempotency. Stateful services depend on or modify the system state. Spawn, teleport_absolute, and set_pen are stateful: spawn creates a new entity, teleport modifies the turtle's position relative to its current state, and set_pen changes drawing state. A misconception is assuming that all services are stateful. Treating an actually stateless service as stateful can introduce unnecessary coordination complexity. When designing your own services, declare clearly whether the call is intended to be idempotent and document how repeated calls should behave so clients can safely retry if needed. Stateless vs Stateful services means stateless services yield the same effect regardless of prior state; stateful services change or depend on system state and require careful handling.. In practical terms, how to tell which category a service belongs to. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Stateless vs Stateful
Stateless services
  • /reset and /clear — no request data, same effect each call.
  • Good for idempotent operations and safe retries.
  • Easy to test from scripts and the command line.
Design tip: prefer stateless semantics when possible to simplify client retry logic.
Stateful services
  • /spawn — creates a new turtle and changes system state.
  • /turtle1/teleport_absolute — moves the turtle to a position; result depends on current pose.
  • /turtle1/set_pen — changes pen color and width, affecting subsequent drawing.
Misconception check: stateful services are not wrong; they need clear documentation about repeated calls and side effects.

screens.title: Battery monitor: combining topics and services
screens.narratorSegment: The battery monitor example demonstrates a common ROS pattern: one node publishes continuous state on a topic and another node subscribes and calls a service when a condition occurs. In the chapter example, the monitor subscribes to /battery_state and checks the percentage. If the battery drops below a threshold, the monitor calls the /set_led service to turn on the red LED. This pattern is useful because topics stream sensor data without blocking, while the service performs a discrete state change with immediate confirmation. A common mistake is trying to stream LED commands on a topic; that complicates the protocol. Instead, publish sensor state on topics and use services for single, state-changing commands. In the walkthrough you will see how the client waits for the service with rospy. wait_for_service, creates a ServiceProxy, and uses it inside the callback. Also note how the code tracks led_on to avoid repeated identical calls and to make the calls effectively idempotent. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Battery Monitor
Excerpt: BatteryMonitor client
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from my_first_robot.srv import SetLed
from sensor_msgs.msg import BatteryState

class BatteryMonitor:
    def __init__(self):
        self.low_battery_threshold = 20
        rospy.wait_for_service('/set_led')
        self.set_led = rospy.ServiceProxy('/set_led', SetLed)
        self.sub = rospy.Subscriber('/battery_state', BatteryState, self.callback)
        self.led_on = False

    def callback(self, msg):
        if msg.percentage < self.low_battery_threshold and not self.led_on:
            self.set_led(3, True)
            self.led_on = True
Explanation & tips
  • wait_for_service ensures the /set_led server exists before calling.
  • ServiceProxy wraps the service for synchronous calls inside the callback.
  • Tracking led_on prevents unnecessary repeated calls and supports idempotency.
Misconception: calling services in a subscriber callback is fine for quick operations, but avoid long-blocking service calls inside callbacks.

screens.title: Service-based robot control patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Service-based control is a lightweight architecture for discrete commands in a robot system. Imagine a controller node that offers services such as /gripper/close, /set_mode, or /save_map. Client nodes—like a teleoperation node, a mission planner, or a health monitor—call these services to change robot state. For example, during low battery the battery monitor calls /set_led; during object pickup the perception node calls /gripper/close and waits for success. The advantage of services here is synchronous confirmation: the caller knows immediately whether the gripper engaged. A clear design approach is to expose short, fast services for discrete effects and reserve actions for long-running tasks that need feedback and preemption. Keep service payloads small and responses informative, including a boolean success and an error string when useful. This approach keeps responsibilities separated and makes the system easier to test and debug. Service-based robot control patterns means expose short, well-defined services for discrete robot commands; clients call them to request state changes and handle immediate success or failure.. In practical terms, how services fit into a robot control architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Service design best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Good service design improves reliability and debuggability. The chapter lists several practical recommendations. First, keep services fast: if a call takes too long, convert the operation into an action to provide feedback and allow preemption. Second, make services idempotent when possible so clients can retry safely. For instance, setting an LED to on should produce the same end-state whether called once or multiple times. Third, include success flags and error messages in responses so clients can react logically rather than guessing. Fourth, avoid using services for high-frequency streaming; topics are the right tool for that. Finally, document expected side effects and whether calls change global state. Applying these practices in turtlesim means designing your own servers — such as a gripper server — to return a boolean success and an optional message, and to perform short, predictable operations. Service design best practices means design services to be fast, idempotent, and to return clear success and error information so clients can handle retries safely.. screens.title: Design question: topic, service, or action?
screens.narratorSegment: A common assessment asks which ROS communication primitive fits a mode switch between manual and autonomous control. The correct choice is a service. A mode switch is a discrete command that changes the robot's operating state, and the caller needs immediate confirmation that the mode change succeeded. A topic would be asynchronous and would not give the caller a synchronous success response, making it hard for the caller to know when the switch actually took effect. An action is designed for long-running tasks that need feedback and the ability to preempt; switching modes is usually quick and does not need continuous feedback, so an action would be overkill. When you make this decision, also apply design best practices: ensure the /set_mode service returns a boolean success and an error string, and make mode switching idempotent whenever possible so retries are safe under network issues. Design question: topic, service, or action? means mode switches are discrete and should use a service for synchronous confirmation; use actions only for long-running tasks needing feedback.. Guided decision
Topic: continuous, publish/subscribe telemetry or high-rate state.
Service: discrete, synchronous commands like /set_mode.
Action: long-running tasks with feedback and preemption.
Apply this rule: if the caller requires immediate confirmation and the operation completes quickly, use a service. If the operation is long and must report progress, use an action. If you need continuous data, use a topic.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore ROS services using the simple turtlesim simulator so you can practice real service patterns before moving to physical robots. You will learn which turtlesim services are available, how to call them from the command line, and how to write a client that uses a service to change robot state. We will also examine service design best practices: keeping calls fast, making them idempotent, and providing clear success or error responses. Along the way you'll see a practical example pattern: a battery monitor subscribes to a topic and calls an LED service when the battery is low. That pattern — topic for continuous state, service for discrete commands — is central to many robot systems like gripper control, mode switching, and calibration routines. By the end of this chapter you should be able to call turtlesim services, write simple service clients and servers, and decide when a state-changing operation belongs in a service rather than a topic or an action.

These objectives guide practice and assessment. First, you will use turtlesim services to teleport, reset, and spawn turtles. Practicing those commands gives you concrete control over simulator state and prepares you to write service clients. Second, you will implement a service-based control system for a simple simulated robot such as a BB-8 or TurtleBot. That means wiring a server to change state and a client or monitor to call those services when needed. Both of these objectives emphasize practical scripting and debugging skills. Third, you will contrast stateless and stateful services so you can choose the right abstraction in your designs. Stateless calls perform an action without depending on current state; stateful calls modify and depend on the simulator or robot state. Finally, you will apply services to real robot scenarios such as LED control, grippers, and mode switching, understanding why services are preferred for discrete, synchronous commands. Each objective maps to hands-on practice: command line calls, Python client code, and a service server skeleton to test.

This second objectives slide emphasizes practice habits and design decisions. You will practice both command-line calls and Python coding so you become fluent with the service workflow: discover the service, inspect its type, call it manually, then automate it with a client. For design, adopt three habits: prefer services for quick, synchronous commands; make responses include success flags and clear error messages; and keep services idempotent so retries are safe. Practically, you will test a simulated gripper service with positions and verify responses, and you will write automation that spawns a second turtle, draws shapes using topics, and uses services to clean up. These practice tasks teach both debugging skills and architectural judgment: how to decide between topic, service, or action when building robot behaviors. Learning Objectives — Practice & Design means combine command-line practice with python automation and adopt idempotent, fast service design.. In practical terms, skills to practice and design principles to adopt. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A ROS service is a synchronous, request-response communication primitive for discrete operations. Unlike topics, which stream data continuously, a service call is a single request that expects a specific reply. This makes services ideal for actions like resetting a simulator, spawning a new entity, or switching a robot's operating mode where the caller needs immediate confirmation. For example, in turtlesim the /reset service uses the std_srvs/Empty type and performs a clear reset with no payload. Another example is /spawn: the client sends x, y, theta, and name in the request and receives the created turtle's name in the response. A common misconception is to use services for frequent, high-rate updates; services are not suited for streaming telemetry. If you need continuous feedback, topics or actions are a better fit. Remember that services should be designed to execute quickly — if the task is long-running with feedback, prefer an action. To solidify this concept, try calling /clear and /reset in turtlesim and observe the immediate, synchronous change. What are ROS services? means services are request-response calls for discrete, synchronous commands; use them when the client needs to know the result immediately.. In practical terms, a definition, behavior, and simple examples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Before you call a service, discover it and inspect its type. Start with rosservice list to see available services and then rosservice type or rosservice info to view the request and response fields. For example, run rosservice list and filter with grep turtlesim to see services like /reset, /spawn, /kill, and /turtle1/teleport_absolute. Once you know the type, craft the right YAML-formatted request and use rosservice call. Practically, spawning a turtle requires sending x, y, theta and name. Teleporting may require floats for x, y, theta depending on the Teleport service definition. A common pitfall is misformatting the YAML payload; watch indentation and quoting for strings. Another pitfall is calling a service before its server is available; use rosservice call only after a node has advertised the service or use rosservice wait. These discovery steps are small but crucial for reliable testing and scripting. Discovering and calling turtlesim services means always inspect available services and their types before calling them; format your request correctly and ensure the server is available.. In practical terms, from rosservice list to rosservice call. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding whether a service is stateless or stateful helps you reason about consistency and retries. Stateless services perform an action that does not depend on existing internal state. Examples in turtlesim include /reset and /clear: calling them produces the same effect regardless of prior simulator state. These services are easy to reason about and are good candidates for idempotency. Stateful services depend on or modify the system state. Spawn, teleport_absolute, and set_pen are stateful: spawn creates a new entity, teleport modifies the turtle's position relative to its current state, and set_pen changes drawing state. A misconception is assuming that all services are stateful. Treating an actually stateless service as stateful can introduce unnecessary coordination complexity. When designing your own services, declare clearly whether the call is intended to be idempotent and document how repeated calls should behave so clients can safely retry if needed. Stateless vs Stateful services means stateless services yield the same effect regardless of prior state; stateful services change or depend on system state and require careful handling.. In practical terms, how to tell which category a service belongs to. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The battery monitor example demonstrates a common ROS pattern: one node publishes continuous state on a topic and another node subscribes and calls a service when a condition occurs. In the chapter example, the monitor subscribes to /battery_state and checks the percentage. If the battery drops below a threshold, the monitor calls the /set_led service to turn on the red LED. This pattern is useful because topics stream sensor data without blocking, while the service performs a discrete state change with immediate confirmation. A common mistake is trying to stream LED commands on a topic; that complicates the protocol. Instead, publish sensor state on topics and use services for single, state-changing commands. In the walkthrough you will see how the client waits for the service with rospy. wait_for_service, creates a ServiceProxy, and uses it inside the callback. Service-based control is a lightweight architecture for discrete commands in a robot system. Imagine a controller node that offers services such as /gripper/close, /set_mode, or /save_map. Client nodes—like a teleoperation node, a mission planner, or a health monitor—call these services to change robot state. For example, during low battery the battery monitor calls /set_led; during object pickup the perception node calls /gripper/close and waits for success. The advantage of services here is synchronous confirmation: the caller knows immediately whether the gripper engaged. A clear design approach is to expose short, fast services for discrete effects and reserve actions for long-running tasks that need feedback and preemption. Keep service payloads small and responses informative, including a boolean success and an error string when useful. This approach keeps responsibilities separated and makes the system easier to test and debug. Good service design improves reliability and debuggability. The chapter lists several practical recommendations. First, keep services fast: if a call takes too long, convert the operation into an action to provide feedback and allow preemption. Second, make services idempotent when possible so clients can retry safely. For instance, setting an LED to on should produce the same end-state whether called once or multiple times. Third, include success flags and error messages in responses so clients can react logically rather than guessing. Fourth, avoid using services for high-frequency streaming; topics are the right tool for that. Finally, document expected side effects and whether calls change global state. A common assessment asks which ROS communication primitive fits a mode switch between manual and autonomous control. The correct choice is a service. A mode switch is a discrete command that changes the robot's operating state, and the caller needs immediate confirmation that the mode change succeeded. A topic would be asynchronous and would not give the caller a synchronous success response, making it hard for the caller to know when the switch actually took effect. An action is designed for long-running tasks that need feedback and the ability to preempt; switching modes is usually quick and does not need continuous feedback, so an action would be overkill. When you make this decision, also apply design best practices: ensure the /set_mode service returns a boolean success and an error string, and make mode switching idempotent whenever possible so retries are safe under network issues. Fourth, design services to be fast, idempotent, and to return informative success or error information so clients can retry safely.
